newsitem.title: BRAZIL: BRAZIL STATE FIRMS IMPROVE PERFORMANCE-FGV.
newsitem.headline: BRAZIL STATE FIRMS IMPROVE PERFORMANCE-FGV.

text.p: Brazil's public sector corporations improved their performance in 1996 as a result of the government's privatization drive and a booming telecoms sector, according to figures published by the independent research institute Getulio Vargas Foundation (FGV).

The figures accompanying the FGV's annual ranking of Brazil's largest 500 corporations show that the 75 state-owned companies included in the list decreased their combined net losses by 35.09 percent in 1996 to 2.34 billion reais ($2.17 billion).
In 1995, 81 public sector firms were included in the list of the 500 largest corporations, with combined losses amounting to 3.61 billion reais ($3.34 billion).

"You can notice a certain improvement in the public sector," said Sergio Gustavo da Costa, head of the FGV company statistics department. "State firms are adjusting to privatization; that's why they are performing better.
"A significant improvement in the results of telecommunications companies was also a major factor in boosting the overall public sector performance," he added.
He said higher telecom tariffs and the start of the sector's privatization had boosted companies' performance.
Of the 10 largest corporations in Brazil only three are in the private sector, with state-owned oil and gas giant Petrobras being the largest corporation in Brazil.

Recently privatized mining conglomerate Companhia Vale do Rio Doce (CVRD) is the largest private sector corporation in Brazil and the sixth largest corporation overall. It also posted the largest 1996 net profit of all the private companies at 517 million reais ($478.7 million).

Sao Paulo state-owned telecoms firm Telesp posted the largest net profit among public sector companies in 1996 at 812.9 million reais ($752.7 million), followed by Petrobras and long distance telephone operator Embratel.

The biggest loss maker among state firms was Sao Paulo state-owned railway Fepasa, with a net loss of 1.39 billion reais ($1.29 billion) in 1996, and among private companies steelmaker Acos Villares posted the largest net loss at 224.1 million reais ($207.5 million).

In 1996, a slightly larger proportion of the top 500 companies posted losses -- 152 versus 149 in 1995 -- but overall combined profits soared 50.17 percent to 5.3 billion reais ($4.91 billion) from 3.53 billion reais ($3.27 billion) in 1995 as a result of the improved public sector performance, Costa said.
